name: SiFive, Inc.
subcategory: RISC-V processor IP and fabless semiconductor
origin_detail: Founded September 2015 in the Bay Area by UC Berkeley RISC-V creators Krste Asanovic, Yunsup Lee and Andrew Waterman, commercialising the open RISC-V ISA and Berkeley's Rocket Chip generator.
openness_notes: Hardware column. In 2016 SiFive released the Chisel RTL and FPGA build flows of its first platforms (Freedom E300 and U500) as open source (Apache-2.0), building on the BSD-licensed Berkeley Rocket Chip generator, so its first products had open design files (3). Its revenue products since 2017 are proprietary, licensed and royalty-bearing core IP built on the open ISA; the Freedom repository was archived on 2021-03-02 and is no longer maintained. Today the ISA is open, older RTL and SDKs are open, and current cores are closed (2). Board-level design files for HiFive boards were not verified.

relicensing_events.from: Open-source Freedom SoC platform (Apache-2.0), actively maintained

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Not a relicence of existing code: the open platform was frozen and the business is proprietary IP on an open ISA. Open RTL remains available read-only.

risk_events: 2021: Intel reportedly offered more than $2B to acquire SiFive (Bloomberg, anonymous source); talks collapsed and SiFive stayed independent
2022: sold its OpenFive custom-silicon unit to Alphawave IP for $210M
2023: laid off about 20% of staff (roughly 130-140 people) and refocused product lines
2023: revenue of $38.2M against a $113.1M operating loss (Bloomberg, from documents it reviewed)
2026: raised $400M Series G, described by the CEO as its final private round before an IPO
robustness: The ISA it depends on is governed by RISC-V International rather than SiFive, so customers can switch to other RISC-V core vendors or open cores; SiFive's moat is implementation quality, not control of the standard. Heavily VC-funded and loss-making as of 2023, but well capitalised after the 2026 round.
physical_science_relevance: RISC-V cores appear in research instruments, accelerators and microcontrollers; the open ISA and open cores such as Rocket enable academic chip tape-outs without licence fees.
openness_effect_assessment: Building on an open, royalty-free ISA let three academics found a processor-IP company that drew a reported $2B Intel approach within six years and a $3.65B valuation by 2026. Openness of the ISA lowered barriers for SiFive and for its competitors alike, so SiFive moved quickly from open RTL to proprietary cores to capture value. Revenue is still small relative to valuation ($38M in 2023), suggesting value rests on the expected growth of the RISC-V ecosystem rather than on SiFive's own open designs.
key_takeaway: SiFive is the clearest example of open-standard, closed-implementation hardware: the open RISC-V ISA created the market, while SiFive's own open-source platform was archived once it had served as a launch vehicle. It shows that an open specification can support a multi-billion-dollar US company, but the money comes from proprietary IP, long timelines and repeated large VC rounds, not from selling open designs.
